title: Why the Ebola Outbreak Keeps Growing, According to Virus Expert Pardis Sabeti
author: Alice Park
body:
The ongoing Ebola outbreak centered in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is now the second largest on record. The virus has infected more than 11,000 people in five countries and has killed more than 5,700 people as of Nov. 20.

Pardis Sabeti, a leader at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard who specializes in computational genetics and evolutionary biology, has tracked Ebola outbreaks for years. In the largest Ebola outbreak on record, in West Africa from 2014 to 2016, she sequenced many of the viral samples from patients, which helped scientists understand how the virus was spreading. Her lab continues to be involved in providing rapid genetic information when viruses strike.

In a conversation with TIME, she explains why the current outbreak grew out of control so quickly—and what would need to change in order for us to finally get ahead of outbreaks like this.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Why is this Ebola outbreak so challenging to control?

In conflict zones like in the DRC, you have the dual problem of an increase in the threats and drivers of infectious-disease spread. You have movement, you have refugees, you have poor sanitation and a breakdown of the health care infrastructure. You have a lot of things going on that are drivers of infectious disease, and it leads to the outbreak spiraling out of control.

At the same time, you’ve taken away all of the surveillance, support, and infrastructure to be aware of infectious diseases spreading. That’s why we didn’t hear about this outbreak until it escalated way out of control. That’s part of the reason it took so long to find out about this outbreak, because of all those breakdowns in this conflict zone—and why it’s so difficult to contain.

It has a lot of things going against it. We have global health funding slashed all around world—and from the U.S., in particular—which cut lots of programs directly in DRC. There are also a lot of rogue groups circulating in the DRC and that makes it really hard for [health] teams to go in and do support.

We’re getting into a situation where the driving risk factors are going up and making it impossible for anybody to work functionally [there] and making it very, very challenging to respond.

Were you surprised that this outbreak was caused by a less common strain of Ebola, Bundibugyo?

Not really. There are a lot of different versions of this virus that circulate. To me, I keep asking, Why do we not have a working diagnostic for all of the different variants of Ebola that we know could easily come about? They’re all related to each other, and once we know one version of the virus, we should be ready to detect every version of that virus that can cause outbreaks. It’s not like this version has never caused an outbreak. It’s not as common, but it has caused outbreaks in the past.

Why do we still chase outbreaks rather than get ahead of them?

Ultimately, in my mind, it’s a challenge of funding and interest. Try as we might, we never get the kind of funding and support to know what is circulating and how we can do this better. There is also still stigmatization surrounding outbreaks. The fact is that a lot of countries don’t want you to know they have outbreaks, because they’re afraid you won’t come to visit. There are so many things driving us not to do what is sensible.

A colleague of mine did a survey that showed in 21 different countries with different cultures, it didn’t matter who you were: everyone hid when they were sick. If that’s true, what are we even doing [in public health]? Literally that’s the premise of what we are trying to do—think about transparency, getting diagnosed, and getting test results. But most people don’t want to come to attention. That’s wild.

How do we change that mentality?

We want to shift how people think about infectious diseases and why we are more afraid of each other than of a bug that could kill us. We just need a lot more outbreak education, in my mind.

Operation Outbreak is an education and communications tool: a simulation of how an outbreak spreads, how we make choices about getting diagnosed, why you want to get vaccinated, and what risks we need to weigh. We teach the basics of recognizing symptoms, how to understand prevalence of a disease, and fundamental epidemiology. It was born from our obsession with Bluetooth-based contact tracing from the Ebola outbreak in 2015. A postdoc in my group was working on creating apps, and we realized that if you give people information that is useful to them then and there, then they are likely to work with us and provide accurate information about their contacts and potential exposures.

We are now working with 27 U.S. states and 20 countries, and we’ve done simulations at the U.N., the World Health Organization, and the FBI. If we want to respond, we need to practice and run simulations like we do for a lot of other things.

The chief minister of Sierra Leone said Operation Outbreak is something he would like to have all of his high school students go through as part of their basic education. And we’re in talks with the governments of Canada and the U.K. The U.S. is more challenging, but more states are getting on board: Utah is planning a big simulation in March 2027 across five schools and colleges, and we have a big partnership with North Carolina as well. We’re constantly working on finding ways to make the information easy to uptake and get out to the public.

Are we getting better at detecting and tracking and ultimately containing infectious disease outbreaks?

We have had so many warning shots fired [by viruses], and we just keep letting them go. International travel will shut down during another outbreak unless we put in place things to track passengers. Travel is such a perfect place to put in place really good surveillance tools that won’t affect a smooth travel experience and let people go about their business, like a quick febrile check or a quick swab. Don’t you want to find out early if you have Ebola?

Let’s just start with saying that none of us want to die from a virus. None of us want our liberties put in jeopardy, but we also don’t want to die. One of the more valuable things that comes out of Operation Outbreak is really talking through our logic frame: are we really so broken as a species that we can’t actually come together on anything? To me it seems [public health] should be a unifying thing.

There’s a real-world example of how important such monitoring is to pick up and contain the spread of Ebola when we look at how the first cases of this outbreak spread to Nigeria and Kenya.

What did the genetic sequences of the viruses from these two people reveal?

We have pretty clear evidence that these two people spread Ebola from one to another, likely in the Ugandan airport. Everything lines up—their [genetic] sequences are very, very close, so it looks like direct transmission in the airport on the same day. One person was clearly quite infectious; their flights left about the same time. That points to airport transmission.

People who turn to public-health officials—and experts like you—for advice on how they can best protect themselves during an outbreak want certainty. Can scientists provide that type of definitive advice?

I literally don’t know all the answers. People want somebody who gives them certainty, but I don’t want certainty. I want somebody to tell me where we’re at. In an outbreak, we should feel like we’re in a group project, and we should all be figuring things out together.
